title: From machine signals to solid-state switches
summary: A ten-section introduction to voltage, junctions, transistors and inductive loads, with a knowledge check and a paper worksheet.

blocks.title: Signals to switches
blocks.body: You already understand a command, a mechanism and a load. Learn what changes when silicon controls the current. By the end, distinguish voltage from current, explain a diode, and tell a MOSFET control signal from a load supply. This is a conceptual lesson and paper exercise; it does not specify a circuit to wire or a machine modification.

blocks.heading: 1. Name the quantity before the number
blocks.body: Voltage is a difference in electric potential between two points. Current is the rate of charge flow through a path. Resistance relates them for a resistor: I = V / R. In an ideal paper example, 12 V across 1,000 ohms gives 0.012 A, or 12 mA. Power is V × I, so that resistor dissipates 0.144 W. These equations describe that resistor; a diode or transistor does not behave like a fixed resistor in every operating region. When someone says “the signal is 3.3 V,” ask: relative to which reference, and driving what input?

blocks.heading: 2. A junction makes direction matter
blocks.body: Doping changes the available charge carriers in silicon. Where p-type and n-type regions meet, a depletion region forms. Forward bias reduces the barrier and permits substantial current; reverse bias normally permits only small leakage until breakdown. A diode uses this asymmetric behavior. “About 0.7 V” is a rough silicon-junction model, not a universal turn-on specification: the drop depends on current, temperature and device construction. Think of a check valve only as a direction analogy; a real diode still has losses and limits. See Toshiba, Chapters I and II, in the source card below.

blocks.heading: 3. Two ways to control a current path

columns.name: Bipolar transistor: base, collector, emitter
columns.detail: A BJT uses base drive to control collector current. In its active region, collector current is approximately current gain times base current. Switching also involves cut-off and saturation, so that gain rule is not a complete switch-design method. The load supply provides the load energy. See Toshiba, Chapter III.

columns.name: MOSFET: gate, drain, source
columns.detail: For an enhancement-mode N-channel MOSFET, gate-to-source voltage controls conduction. The gate is insulated, but switching requires charging and discharging it. Threshold voltage marks the start of conduction at a specified test current; it does not promise low on-resistance at your load current. Check the specified gate voltage for RDS(on). See the TI gate-drive report.

blocks.heading: 4. Follow the energy through a valve command
items: Conceptual example: a controller requests a valve to move. Its logic signal reaches a suitable driver, while a separate supply provides the coil current. A logic output is not a substitute for the load supply.
With the switch on, coil current builds and energy is stored in the magnetic field. Component losses turn some supplied power into heat.
At turn-off, inductive current cannot disappear instantly. The circuit needs a designed path or clamp for the stored energy; otherwise voltage can rise enough to damage the switch.

A freewheeling diode is one possible approach. A low clamp voltage generally releases the coil more slowly than a higher-voltage clamp. Protection and release time must be designed together. See the TI inductive-load source.

Before choosing actual hardware, identify load current, supply and transient limits, driver capability, thermal conditions and the equipment’s required stop behavior. This lesson supplies no component ratings or wiring design.

blocks.heading: 5. Does a 2 V threshold settle it?
blocks.prompt: A hypothetical MOSFET lists a 2 V threshold, but its low RDS(on) is specified only at 10 V gate-to-source. Is a 3.3 V control signal enough to guarantee that low resistance?
options: Yes, because 3.3 V is above the threshold.
No. Check guaranteed on-resistance at the intended gate drive and the load conditions.
Yes, if the load uses a separate supply.
blocks.explanation: Threshold is measured near the start of conduction. It does not establish low resistance at the intended current. A separate load supply is necessary in many designs, but it does not fix insufficient gate drive. Revisit section 3 and the TI gate-drive report.

items.label: Separate control and power
items.detail: On paper, name the command signal, driver, switch, load, supply and reference. Describe each role; this is not a wiring schematic.

items.label: Explain the diode
items.detail: Say what forward and reverse bias mean, then name one reason a fixed 0.7 V assumption can fail.

items.label: Explain the gate specification
items.detail: State why threshold and the gate voltage used to specify RDS(on) answer different questions.

items.label: Account for turn-off energy
items.detail: Describe where an inductive load’s stored energy goes and why release time matters.

items.label: Save your explanation elsewhere
items.detail: Write one uncertain point and your answer to the quiz in your own notes. This prototype does not save learning results; navigating away from a block in Present can reset its answers and checks.
